Ossoff did not directly respond, and he again pointed to the fact that those close to Collins amplified white nationalists’ posts.

“How weak a person do you have to be to be unable to stop someone under your own roof from disseminating neo-Nazi propaganda while you run for Senate?” Ossoff said. “The paper reported it’s still going on today.”
Given a chance to respond, Collins did not address it directly. But he said rhetoric like Ossoff’s had motivated a New York man who is accused of making death threats against him.
“I’m a little tired of this, Jon,” Collins said. “This crazy person is in jail right now because of your rhetoric.”
Neither candidate directly answered the other’s charges.

Collins also, once again, did not answer questions about whether or not Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election. He was asked about audio of a call Trump made after the 2020 election asking Georgia Republican Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “find 11,780 votes” to help overturn the 2020 election.
“You know, Joe Biden went into office, and boy, Georgians paid for it,” Collins said.

title: Ukraine says new Starlink restrictions disrupt military as it reels from intel gaps and Trump clash
summary: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of disrupting its military operations by limiting Starlink internet services, as the country reeled from a pair of intense Russian missile attacks that it said came without the usual advance warning from allies.
story: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of disrupting its military operations by limiting Starlink internet services, as the country reeled from a pair of intense Russian missile attacks that it said came without the usual advance warning from allies.

Facing pressure from President Donald Trump to halt strikes on Russia’s energy industry, Kyiv and its backers have worried Washington could cut off battlefield support to try and force it into concessions at the negotiating table.

Ukrainian officials and their European partners were already scrambling to understand the status of U.S. intelligence sharing after the lack of alert ahead of two Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv this week caused confusion, two Ukrainian and two European officials told NBC News.

Trump insisted the U.S. was still sharing intel, but with relations spiraling Ukrainian officials and military units were on Wednesday accusing SpaceX of throttling a technology essential to their battlefield communications and drone operations.
It was not immediately clear what might be behind the Starlink interruptions, though some Ukrainian officials said the timing could not be a coincidence given that Musk is a close Trump ally.
Drone disruptions

SpaceX had introduced speed limits on the operation of its Starlink satellite internet terminals overnight, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s defense tech adviser, Serhii Beskrestnov.

“Our defence forces received no warning of such a restriction, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” Beskrestnov said on Telegram. “It is obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” he added.
An army unit fighting in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region said Wednesday it had been forced to cancel some planned operations.

The 7th Rapid Reaction Corps of the Ukrainian air assault forces said it began “noticing Starlink connectivity problems caused by data transfer speed limits” overnight, adding that the changes directly affected drones that use the service for in-flight control.
“The drones kept flying, but the interruptions made them harder to control,” it said in a statement.
Beskrestnov said that restrictions were specifically put on the operation of the military-grade version of Starlink at speeds above 100 mph.

Starlink was also key for Ukraine’s aerial defenses as it was used to intercept the jet-powered drones that Moscow has unleashed on Ukrainian cities in recent months, he added. Asked about the importance of the technology, Ukraine’s Charge d’Affaires to the U.S. Denys Sienik said “the technology helps us save the lives of civilians and prevent more destruction in Ukraine caused by the Russian side.”

title: Texas DA says ICE intentionally hit immigrant with a car and may have withheld evidence
summary: Harris County DA Sean Teare told NBC News his office has collected multiple videos for its own investigation but isn’t getting cooperation from the federal government.
story: HOUSTON — Videos collected by local investigators make it “pretty obvious” that an ICE officer intentionally ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez during an immigration stop Saturday, which could lead to assault charges, the district attorney said Tuesday.

“This was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told NBC News.

Teare said the federal government is not cooperating with the investigation conducted by his office and the Harris County Sheriff’s Office. He also said ICE may have allowed the erasure of critical data in the vehicle involved in striking Parra, who was on foot.

Teare said that in his seven years as a Harris County vehicular crimes division chief, he has reviewed video from a number of other auto-pedestrian collision cases. He said the video his investigators have gathered in Parra’s case “goes above” the video that was posted online and obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston.

“My viewing of it, and many other investigators that have viewed it, as well, it’s pretty obvious that this was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” he said.

Parra, 48, was left with multiple breaks and fractures in his body, according to his attorney and an advocate who has been speaking on his behalf. He had surgery on one leg and faces multiple additional operations, said Cesar Espinosa, co-founder and executive director of FIEL, an immigrant civil rights group.

Video obtained by KPRC shows a white truck headed in the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. It shows a vehicle jumping a yellow median and heading in the direction that Parra is running.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

It then appears to show the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center. The parked truck leaves, and a man can be seen on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows.
An ICE spokesman said over the weekend that officers were pursuing the fleeing men and that “Miguel Parra Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”
Teare, a Democrat, announced late Monday that his office had launched an independent investigation.

On Tuesday, an ICE spokesperson who was not identified said in a statement that “allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct.”

ICE said the allegations are “disgusting smears” that are “peddled by the media,” leading to more than a 1,600% increase in assaults and a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks against its law enforcement officers. It did not offer data behind those numbers.

ICE has said that Parra was not the target of the attempted stop but that he was in the country illegally. Parra’s attorney and family have said he has no criminal record and was on his way to work applying stucco.

Teare said his office and the sheriff’s office determined that the vehicle that struck Parra was a Jeep Cherokee and that it potentially had evidence, including a data crash recorder. He said his office wanted to know whether the vehicle locked in information at the time of the collision that could be downloaded, such as speed, steering and braking. Teare said the way to preserve data from the car would have been to “put it on a flatbed trailer and you take it to forensically download it.”
But he said he believes any data on the recorder related to the incident could have been erased when ICE drove the car away.
He and the sheriff’s investigators told ICE the information needed to be downloaded, but ICE refused, Teare said.
ICE did not respond to questions about a data crash recorder, the erasing of any potential data or any refusal to download it.

“Our office began drafting a search warrant that we were in the process of drafting when the ICE agent in question, the one that had been driving, we believed, at the time of the collision, jumped back into the car and drove it away from the scene,” Teare said. “In my 20-year career, I’ve never heard of anything like that.”

Teare also said two people from “an entirely different operation” were in the back seat of the ICE vehicle when it struck Parra. Those two people are also in ICE custody, along with Parra. Teare said his office is working to ensure all three remain in the country as material witnesses.

“I’ve taught for years at the Houston Police Department Academy, Harris County Department Academy. I’ve worked with law enforcement for 20 years. There is not a single agency in the United States that would teach that once you put people in custody in your car, you then begin to pursue other people,” he said.
Doing so puts “every single person out there in danger again,” he said.
According to Teare, the ICE vehicle should have activated its emergency equipment, such as its lights and siren, as it jumped a median and crossed into oncoming traffic.

A senior official at the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News on Tuesday that multiple ICE officers on the scene at the time were wearing body cameras. ICE is reviewing video of the scene as part of an internal investigation, the official said.
Espinosa said Parra told him that he fled because it was unclear whether there were officials in the vehicles, which he said were unmarked, did not use sirens and had dark, tinted windows.

ICE has said it was targeting another man, Jose Mendoza Cervantes, who was in the country illegally and had committed several crimes. Espinoza and Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno said neither Parra nor the man who was with him when ICE stopped their vehicle has any association with Mendoza.

In previous encounters between ICE and targets of its arrests in vehicle stops, including some who have been killed, such as Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, ICE has alleged the people it tried to arrest weaponized their vehicles.
Parra was struck less than two weeks after the Trump administration issued guidance setting tighter rules for vehicle stops.

The guidance says only agents who have completed specific training should make vehicle stops. The memo also says that vehicles used for traffic stops must have lights and sirens and that all officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras.

The Harris County District Attorney’s Office has been asking witnesses and people who may have photos or video of the incident to contact it. Teare said that there is a secure portal that goes directly to the district attorney’s office and that no one is asked about citizenship or immigration status.
“All we are interested in is getting the truth, and any shred of cellphone footage, anyone that saw something and really can point us in the right direction, it would be wonderful,” he said.

title: Romance scammers are getting harder to catch. The consequences are costly.
summary: For people looking for love online, a match with a scammer could cost them their life savings.
story: For people looking for love online, a match with a scammer could cost them their life savings.

A congressional investigation, which began in September 2025 and lasted about a year, found that Tinder’s scam detection systems struggled for years to keep fraudulent accounts off the dating app. Parent company Match Group has since moved to address the shortcomings with new verification requirements and upgraded detection technology.
Romance scams have become a leading form of financial fraud in the U.S., costing Americans nearly $1.5 billion in reported losses last year, according to the Federal Trade Commission.

“There’s a lot of stigma to being a victim to scams,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who launched the investigation alongside Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in an interview last week. “People should understand that really sophisticated people who are doing all the right things are still getting scammed because of the level of technology and resources that these criminal enterprises now do.”

Scammers today can realistically pose as representatives from familiar organizations like the local YMCA or a bank, and the accessibility of AI tools makes it easier than ever to research family members and mimic their voices. But romance scams, Hassan said, can be particularly emotionally devastating.

That was the case for Pennsylvania resident Sue Nuss, who told Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship after she lost her husband. There, she met a man who claimed to be from New Jersey.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened.
-Sue nuss, who spoke to Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship.
Nuss told NBC News that, over a month and a half, he won her trust with words that made her feel like he really “sees” and “understands” her.

The committee’s report, published Tuesday, stated that the man duped Nuss with a series of “fabricated” crises: job problems on an oil rig, an arrest in Mexico, his mom’s stroke and even her funeral — all excuses to ask Nuss, 77, for money. When the scammers behind the profile tried to trick her into believing the man she was dating had died, she said, she realized it was all a scam.

“I have always been a very giving person my entire life, and I’ve always been a caregiver,” Nuss told NBC News last week. “And I fell prey. I was very vulnerable. I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened.”
Days after what she thought was a budding online relationship fell apart, Nuss’ scammer showed back up on Tinder with the same profile, she said in an interview.

Soon, another group approached her claiming they could recover what she had lost. Then, through an elaborate cryptocurrency scheme, that group managed to scam even more money from Nuss. She believes both scammer groups were connected, the report stated. It added that, in total, she lost more than $700,000.

“I struggle. Some days are really bad days and some days are good days. I do get therapy. I’m starting a very special therapy next week called EMDR because it’s a trauma,” Nuss said. “I don’t trust my decisions now.”

Congress last month passed the Romance Scam Prevention Act, which would require online dating service providers to notify and warn any users who get messaged by potential scammers. The bill awaits President Donald Trump’s signature.

This summer, Hassan also introduced legislation with Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., to create a central reporting portal for victims of scams, an initiative that she said could give the federal government the tools to detect patterns in scams to shut them down more effectively.
Scammers stole more than $1 trillion globally in one year, according to a 2024 report from the Global Anti-Scam Alliance.

“Enterprises that run scams are now costing the global economy more than the illicit drug trade does,” Hassan said. “This is really important for individuals. It’s really important for our economy. And so, the more people speak up about the need to change the way the federal government handles scams, the faster it’s going to happen.”

The Joint Economic Committee’s investigation sought to combat the prevalence of romance scams on platforms owned by Match Group, the biggest online dating company in the world, with a portfolio that includes Tinder, Hinge, Match and Plenty of Fish.

It found that during the first nine months of 2025, nearly 1.5 million scammers or other bad actors on Tinder and Hinge matched with someone. Nearly 500,000 of those accounts then exchanged contact information with other users.

Internal documents shared voluntarily with the committee noted that most of Tinder’s machine-learning detection scam models hadn’t been updated in years, and Match Group staff members found that scammers could quickly circumvent the company’s patchwork detection rules. Excessive false positives also overwhelmed the human moderators trying to detect dangerous accounts.
The committee wrote that it welcomes the changes Match Group has made to address those concerns.

Match Group deployed new detection models throughout the latter half of 2025 and the first half of 2026 to better catch bad actors, according to the committee’s report. This year, it introduced 169 automated rules and “improved” 108 others aimed at targeting and removing inauthentic actors.

One of its key rollouts is a mandatory biometric face check for all new users on Tinder and Hinge, meant to prevent users from making multiple accounts and ensure banned users can’t make new accounts.

Yoel Roth, Match Group’s senior vice president of trust and safety, told NBC News the company is “grateful the Committee recognized our significant advancements to protect our users against romance scams.”

“That said, the report mischaracterizes both the historical scale of our investment and the work already completed. Alongside our engagement with the Committee over the past year, we’ve made the largest safety advancements in Match Group’s history,” Roth wrote in a statement. “Trust and Safety is a foundational priority, and we intend to continue leading the industry in building tools that promote authentic, safe connections.”

Much of that safety work, including the face checks, was already underway before the committee’s investigation, according to Match Group. It reports having seen a roughly 60% reduction in exposure to bad actors in every market since the face checks began.
Hassan similarly said those measures have “already been successful in dramatically reducing the number of matches that their customers have with a scammer.”

“They need to do more, though, because there are still gaps in their systems,” she added. “And they are going to need to stay vigilant in new ways, because the criminals are always changing their technology and their tactics, too.”

title: Ukraine says new Starlink restrictions disrupt military as it reels from intel gaps and Trump clash
summary: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of disrupting its military operations by limiting Starlink internet services, as the country reeled from a pair of intense Russian missile attacks that it said came without the usual advance warning from allies.
story: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of disrupting its military operations by limiting Starlink internet services, as the country reeled from a pair of intense Russian missile attacks that it said came without the usual advance warning from allies.

Facing pressure from President Donald Trump to halt strikes on Russia’s energy industry, Kyiv and its backers have worried Washington could cut off battlefield support to try and force it into concessions at the negotiating table.

Ukrainian officials and their European partners were already scrambling to understand the status of U.S. intelligence sharing after the lack of alert ahead of two Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv this week caused confusion, two Ukrainian and two European officials told NBC News.

Trump insisted the U.S. was still sharing intel, but with relations spiraling Ukrainian officials and military units were on Wednesday accusing SpaceX of throttling a technology essential to their battlefield communications and drone operations.
It was not immediately clear what might be behind the Starlink interruptions, though some Ukrainian officials said the timing could not be a coincidence given that Musk is a close Trump ally.
Drone disruptions

SpaceX had introduced speed limits on the operation of its Starlink satellite internet terminals overnight, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s defense tech adviser, Serhii Beskrestnov.

“Our defence forces received no warning of such a restriction, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” Beskrestnov said on Telegram. “It is obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” he added.
An army unit fighting in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region said Wednesday it had been forced to cancel some planned operations.

The 7th Rapid Reaction Corps of the Ukrainian air assault forces said it began “noticing Starlink connectivity problems caused by data transfer speed limits” overnight, adding that the changes directly affected drones that use the service for in-flight control.
“The drones kept flying, but the interruptions made them harder to control,” it said in a statement.
Beskrestnov said that restrictions were specifically put on the operation of the military-grade version of Starlink at speeds above 100 mph.

Starlink was also key for Ukraine’s aerial defenses as it was used to intercept the jet-powered drones that Moscow has unleashed on Ukrainian cities in recent months, he added. Asked about the importance of the technology, Ukraine’s Charge d’Affaires to the U.S. Denys Sienik said “the technology helps us save the lives of civilians and prevent more destruction in Ukraine caused by the Russian side.”

title: Inflation jumps to 3.7% as gas and diesel prices squeeze consumers ahead of the midterms
summary: Prices rose across broad swaths of the economy in September, as high energy costs triggered by the Iran war pushed up costs in many major consumer categories.
story: Prices rose across broad swaths of the U.S. economy in September, as high energy costs triggered by the Iran war pushed up prices in many major consumer categories.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics said Wednesday that overall prices rose 3.7% from a year ago, and 0.6% from August. Categories including housing, clothing and restaurant and take out food all saw price increases. Only three major categories saw price declines: groceries, medical care commodities and utility gas service.
“The index for gasoline rose 9.1 percent in September, accounting for over half of the monthly all items increase,” the BLS said in its report.

The report adds to ongoing concerns that persistent inflation is taking a toll on consumers, particularly as wage growth has been stagnant. As of September, the growth in wages was pacing at 3% on an annual basis. Paychecks have not grown faster than inflation since March.
The overall increase was slightly more than had been expected by economists polled by Dow Jones, who forecast a jump to 3.6%.
Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, also rose to 2.6% from a year ago, or 0.3% from August. This was also slightly more than had been expected.
Friday’s number is the final inflation report before November’s pivotal midterm elections, in which business owners and consumers have said they will be voting with their bottom line in mind.

Since August, oil prices have risen to more than $106 per barrel from about $80. The price of unleaded gas, which most consumers use, has risen 45% since late February, when the United States and Israel launched the Iran war. The price of diesel, which powers businesses, farms, the shipping industry and other critical sectors, has soared 70% over the same period.

title: Chick-fil-A bet on chicken 60 years ago. Now it’s America’s third largest restaurant chain.
summary: The family-owned company reported nearly $24 billion in sales last year and recently expanded to Singapore and the United Kingdom.
story: For decades, Chick-fil-A — with its iconic cow mascot — has encouraged Americans to skip hamburgers and instead “Eat Mor Chikin.”

Today Chick-fil-A is the third-largest restaurant chain in the U.S. behind McDonald’s and Starbucks, with nearly $24 billion in sales last year. Chick-fil-A also has around 3,000 locations around the world, having recently expanded to the U.K. and Singapore.
But the global giant came from humble beginnings.
“My grandfather grew up in extreme poverty,” CEO Andrew Cathy said in a recent interview for NBC News’ Business in America series.

“He actually lived in the first government housing in the state of Georgia, and after the war, he decided to start a business with his brother Ben. And they’re like, ‘We want a better life for ourselves,’” Cathy said.

So Truett and Ben Cathy opened a diner called the Dwarf Grill in Hapeville, Georgia, in 1946. After a local supplier offered them big chicken breasts that had been rejected by Delta Air Lines, Truett developed the sandwich that eventually became the signature menu item of the first Chick-fil-A restaurant in 1967.
Truett’s son Dan Cathy eventually took over the business from his father, and his son Andrew became CEO in 2021.
For 60 years, Chick-fil-A has remained a private, family-owned business — and Andrew Cathy says it plans to stay that way.
But while much has changed at the company over the decades, its signature chicken sandwich has stayed consistent.
“It’s still the same recipe that we’ve had since 1967,” Cathy said. As for what’s in the recipe, he said: “It’s a lot of good things. Can’t tell you the details.”
Faith in the business
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
But certainly one of the company’s core ingredients has been the Cathy family’s Christian faith.
Chick-fil-A has never been open on Sundays, a decision Cathy said his grandfather and great-uncle made many years ago.

“It was very common back in the 1940s that a lot of places were closed on Sunday,” he said. “They wanted to do that. They wanted to have a chance to take a break, go to church and for others just to take some rest.”

For the Cathys, the business is an expression of their faith. Chick-fil-A’s mission is to “Glorify God by being a faithful steward of all that is entrusted to us. To have a positive influence on all who come in contact with Chick-fil-A.”
But running a business based on Christian values can be challenging in 21st century America.
The Cathys experienced that firsthand in 2012, when Dan Cathy told a religious newspaper that the family supported “the biblical definition of the family unit.”

Cathy’s comments set off an explosion of controversy when Americans were deeply split over the issue of same-sex marriage. Protests and boycotts of Chick-fil-A restaurants across the country were met with counterprotests and “buycotts.”
On Aug. 1 of that year, Chick-fil-A supporters flocked to the restaurant and delivered the company a record-setting “Chick-fil-A Appreciation Day.”
The company has also donated millions of dollars to Christian organizations that drew criticism from advocates for LGBTQ+ rights.
In 2014, Dan Cathy expressed regret over having involved the company in the debate, although he stood by his private views about marriage.
Asked about backlash the company has received on LGBTQ+ issues, Andrew Cathy gave a diplomatic response.
“We’ve always been focused on serving great food and hospitality, and so for anybody that comes in the door, we’re going to continue to do that,” he said.

The Supreme Court legalized same-sex marriage in 2015, and starting in 2020, Chick-fil-A changed its approach to charitable giving — focusing exclusively on the issues of education, homelessness and hunger.

The company’s Shared Table program donates extra food from Chick-fil-A restaurants to local nonprofits that provide meals to people in need. Chick-fil-A says the program has provided more than 200 million meals since 2020.
A value proposition
The company is also navigating an economic environment this year in which millions of Americans have pulled back on dining out.
Consumer prices have jumped 3.4%, while wages have grown just 3% on average — meaning that for many Americans, paychecks aren’t keeping up with rising costs.

Chick-fil-A’s prices aren’t the cheapest on the block, either. At a Chick-fil-A in Dallas, for example, the standard chicken sandwich is $4.99. At a McDonald’s less than a mile down the road, the similar McCrispy sandwich costs $3.99.
But Cathy said Chick-fil-A knows many of its consumers are feeling pinched and making tough choices about where they want to spend their dollars.
“Even though our costs are going up, we’ve got to be careful knowing that consumers are making that trade-off,” he said.
“What we want more than anything is if customers do choose to eat with us, they feel like ‘Man, I got a great value for what I paid for this experience.’”

title: Pope Leo spends a peaceful night in the hospital after cancer surgery
summary: VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV spent a calm night in the hospital after successful surgery that saw part of his right lung removed and a confirmed cancer diagnosis, the Vatican said early Wednesday.
story: VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV spent a calm night in the hospital after successful surgery that saw part of his right lung removed and a confirmed cancer diagnosis, the Vatican said early Wednesday.
It said more information would follow later in the day.
The 71-year-old American pontiff was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer that accounts for 80% of all cases, according to the American Lung Association.

The 90-minute operation to remove a malignant lung nodule was completed “successfully, on schedule and as planned,” the Vatican said Tuesday. Leo was in the operating theater for nearly three hours, it said.
The Vatican did not offer details on planned treatment moving forward or whether the cancer might have spread.

The initial lump was detected during a routine check, the Vatican has said. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics took the rare step of revealing the health issue — the first of his papacy — during his Sunday noon prayer.
Leo waved to crowds outside Rome’s Gemelli hospital as he entered Tuesday.
The procedure was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, with medical staff reciting the rosary prayer in the hospital chapel as the operation began.
The surgery saw the lower lobe of the pope’s right lung removed using a “video-assisted technique,” according to the Vatican.

Following his surgery, the pontiff “woke up normally and, after a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the tenth floor,” the Vatican said. The room is next to the usual papal apartment, complete with private chapel, which is currently undergoing renovations.
This type of cancer affects both smokers and nonsmokers, although Leo is not known to ever have been a smoker.
The cancer diagnosis could complicate his busy schedule.
Just weeks earlier, hundreds of thousands of people packed the streets of Paris for an outdoor mass on a visit that saw Leo warn about the risks of artificial intelligence.
He was planning to take a historic two-week visit to South America next month, although it is unclear if that will still go ahead.
Messages of support and sympathy flowed in after the news.
Dr. Fernando Daniels III, a 67-year-old physician from Maryland  was among many praying for Leo’s swift recovery in the Vatican’s St. Peter’s Square.
“I’ve seen miracles in medicine. I’ve seen people told with terminal illnesses they wouldn’t live and they did,” he told NBC News.
“Prayers of all should heal him,” said Daniels, who was traveling as part of a group.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he and his wife, Jeanette Rubio, were praying for the pope, who was born in Chicago.
“May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father,” Rubio said on X.
“We thank God that the surgery on Pope Leo was, by all accounts, successful, and that he continues his recovery and recuperation,” New York City’s Archbishop Ronald Hicks said in a statement.
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, whose role is largely ceremonial, wished Leo a speedy and full recovery, the German Catholic news agency KNA reported.

“The pope‘s voice on the current issues and challenges of our time is of particular importance and of value to many people worldwide, including in Germany, beyond denominational boundaries,” Steinmeier was quoted as saying.
Claudio Lavanga reported from Vatican City, and Mithil Aggarwal reported from Hong Kong.

title: Federal judge issues longer-term decision blocking Trump’s White House media ban
summary: U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued an injunction preventing CNN, Politico and MS NOW from being booted from the White House grounds until the case is decided.
story: A federal judge issued an order late Tuesday blocking the Trump administration from banning CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House complex while the organizations’ lawsuit over access proceeds.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly of Washington, D.C., issued the preliminary injunction in the wake of a hearing Thursday at which the administration contended it imposed the ban in part because of national security concerns; media organizations said it was because of “viewpoint discrimination.”

Kelly sided with the news outlets, noting that Trump used national security as a reason for the ban after their press passes had already been revoked and ruling that it also likely violated reporters’ freedom of speech and due process rights.

“There is practically nothing national security-related in the record connected to the President’s decision to revoke Plaintiffs’ hard passes to which the Court can defer,” Kelly wrote in his 26-page opinion.

His order will give the outlets access to the White House until the underlying lawsuit challenging the ban is resolved. But it doesn’t require the administration to allow reporters from the outlets access to the Oval Office or Air Force One — locations where the administration has blocked reporters from CNN and Politico in recent weeks.
Trump vowed to appeal on Truth Social before the ruling was handed down. The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment following the ruling.
Kelly had issued a temporary restraining order lifting the ban while he weighed whether to issue an injunction.
Trump announced the bans of CNN, MS NOW and Politico on social media on Sept. 18, saying they were a “result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he wrote on Truth Social.
In court filings, the three news organizations said the ban affected 78 journalists who had “hard passes,” meaning they had been previously screened and credentialed to work at the White House.
The outlets filed a lawsuit alleging Trump’s action violated their due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the suit said.

The White House and Trump then began arguing that the ban was intended to address national security concerns, with Trump saying in another post that the outlets’ reporting was “a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”
For Subscribers
The judge was unmoved by that argument.
Kelly said it was clear from Trump’s announcement of the ban and from subsequent remarks that his motivation was content.

“President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him,” Kelly wrote, finding this decision violated the journalists’ First and Fifth amendment rights.

He noted, however, that his decision doesn’t concede that Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness are unfounded or that the government is “powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.”
For Subscribers

Kelly cited Trump’s recent remarks to Time magazine that he didn’t like “bad story after bad story” coming from CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists. It was, Ted Boutrous, the news outlets’ attorney, had argued ahead of the decision, “a confession of what amounts to viewpoint discrimination.”
“President Trump, I’ll give him credit,” Boutrous said. “He’s not hiding it.”
In his previous decision, Kelly also found that the administration had denied the outlets due process under settled law from several cases that have made their way to the D.C. federal appeals court.
The White House argued that the appeals court decisions were wrong.
“Maybe—but this Court is bound by D.C. Circuit precedent, full stop,” Kelly wrote.

At a hearing on the injunction Thursday, the Justice Department lawyer representing the White House, Michael Velchik, asked Kelly to lift his restraining order, calling the White House a “sacred place” that shouldn’t have to give people access just because they “identify as a reporter.”
“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” Velchik said.

Boutrous argued that the administration was engaging in impermissible and unconstitutional “viewpoint discrimination” because the ban was based on Trump’s dislike of the outlets’ reporting and because he has said he hoped the ban would force journalists to “straighten themselves out.”
In court filings, Boutrous urged Kelly to ignore the national security arguments, saying they were manufactured and not what the case is really about.

Boutrous argued that “the President himself has continued telling anyone who will listen precisely what this ban is really about, most recently complaining at length in an interview with Time magazine that he banned Plaintiffs because he feels that he should not ‘be forced to bear’ what he considers ‘constantly bad stories,’ as he ‘won the election’ and has ‘done great things.’”
After Tuesday night’s ruling, Boutrous said he and his clients were grateful to the court for securing their access anew.

“The President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like,” he said in a statement. “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban.’”

Separately, the Justice Department said last week that it was investigating five major TV networks, including CNN and NBC, for potentially violating federal antitrust laws after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of Trump as a result of the ban against the three news outlets.

The pool is a rotating group of networks that share the duties of recording a president’s activities during public appearances and travel. The on-duty network then distributes information and media, such as video and audio, to other outlets for their use.

title: Dolly Parton’s nephew responds to restraining order, denies threatening violence
summary: Bryan Seaver, Parton’s nephew and former head of security, says the messages submitted to the court were out of context in regard to a payment dispute.
story: Dolly Parton’s nephew denied accusations that he threatened to use violence and destroy his aunt’s legacy, telling the court the messages were taken out of context from a specific business dispute, according to a new court filing.

Bryan Seaver submitted an affidavit on Tuesday in Nashville, Tennessee, in response to a temporary restraining order request by She’s Alive, the entity that manages and protects Parton’s professional property and business. The company had accused Seaver last month of sending increasingly threatening messages and describing himself as an “international arms dealer” as part of the threats.

According to Seaver, the situation arose from a dispute between his security company and the company that operates Dolly’s hotel and museum in downtown Nashville. Seaver’s company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, provided security for the hotel and was owed approximately $251,000 in services rendered, the affidavit said.
“SAPS had not been paid since approximately one to two weeks before Ms. Parton died on August 25, 2026,” Seaver said.

All invoices from Seaver prior to Parton’s death were sent to Danny Nozell, Parton’s longtime manager who runs She’s Alive, he said in the affidavit. The messages referred to in the restraining order were sent directly to Nozell, Seaver said.

Seaver said in his affidavit that the messages were “sent in the course of private conversations between two friends” and that they were never sent to employees of She’s Alive, referred to as “SAL” in the filing.

“I have never threatened physical harm to Mr. Nozell, to any SAL employee, contractor, attorney, advisor, or business partner, or to anyone else associated with SAL,” Seaver said. “I have no intention of doing so.”

Seaver describes his messages to Nozell regarding the alleged threat to ruin Parton’s legacy as part of his frustration at not being paid by the company managing her hotel, Herschend Family Entertainment. He said the podcast conversation was part of a larger discussion on the large number of media requests Seaver received following his aunt’s death, which Nozell was advising him on.

The message from Seaver read, “I’m going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or f------ pay me.”
“They were not a threat made to SAL or any third party. Mr. Nozell never replied that I should not do it or that it was a bad idea,” Seaver said in the affidavit.

Seaver also included screenshots of messages in which he references being an international arms dealer in his filing. Part of Seaver’s security work involves working as an arms broker between the U.S. government and the Haitian National Police, he clarified in the affidavit.
The screenshots in Seaver’s filing include a purported reply from Nozell to the message saying, “You should promote that.”

The messages appear to be in the context of the numerous media requests Seaver has received following Parton’s death. Seaver also wrote, “I just sold 29 million dollars worth of ammo to Haiti. I’m not exactly a media person, Danny,” according to the filing.

Other messages from Seaver included in his filing appear to express a desire to cut the Herschend Family Entertainment out of Parton’s business dealings. Seaver wrote that he would “ratf--- every Herschend entity I can possibly conjure.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
A spokesperson for Herschend Family Entertainment did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Seaver admitted in his affidavit that his language was crude, but said he understood the “slang” to mean “undercut or outmaneuver someone in business or politics.”
“It does not mean physical harm, and I did not intend it that way,” Seaver’s affidavit said. “I have never sent anything to Dollywood or HFE threatening to harm their brand or their personnel.”

Seaver also denied allegations made in court that he attempted to avoid being served legal paperwork in this case by putting barbed wire at his front door and caution tape at his home. He said that the request for barbed wire was actually made by his teenage son while Seaver was working.

“People repeatedly came to our front door, rang the doorbell, knocked, and pulled on the screen door, beginning early in the morning and continuing during the day,” Seaver said. “The media is constantly at my home.”
The barbed wire and tape were put in the home by Seaver’s son and the purpose was to protect the family “from unwanted approaches, not to evade service of process,” the affidavit said.
Seaver’s company has since received the more than $250,000 payment and has been replaced as the security company employed by She’s Alive, according to the affidavit.

In Seaver’s opposition to the restraining order issued earlier this month, he notes that the restrictions are overly broad. The terms say that he cannot have contact or be within 1,000 feet of anyone who “has or may have” a business relationship with She’s Alive.
“I have no way of knowing who all of those people and entities are,” Seaver said. “I could violate the Order without knowing it simply by going about my business in Nashville.”
He also noted that this would likely include his own family members, as his mother, sisters, aunts and cousins have employment or connections to Parton’s estate.
“A restriction extending to everyone who ‘has or may have’ a business relationship with SAL could reach ordinary communications with close family members,” Seaver said.

title: Georgia police identify man who fatally fell off Six Flags roller coaster
summary: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was an employee at Wesley International Academy in the Atlanta Public Schools district, according to the district.
story: Georgia police on Tuesday identified the 42-year-old who died after being ejected from a Six Flags roller coaster outside Atlanta.
The Cobb County Police Department said the incident, which occurred Monday at about 4 p.m. at Six Flags Over Georgia, also left several injured.
Preliminary findings from witness and employee interviews indicate that Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was “ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction.”
When officers arrived at the scene, Kariem was found unresponsive and beneath the ride.
“Investigators continue to examine the circumstances surrounding the incident,” the police statement said.
Several others were injured, according to officials, but it is unclear how many. The department’s Major Crimes Unit is investigating.

Atlanta Public Schools said in a statement that Kariem was a “member of its community” at the Wesley International Academy, an Atlanta public charter school for kindergarten through eighth grade. It is unclear whether Kariem was a teacher, and the district did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The school’s leadership shared a letter with NBC News that it sent to families.

“We know this news is heartbreaking and difficult to process. Mr. Kariem was a valued member of our Wesley family, and his loss will be deeply felt throughout our school community,” the letter said. “Our thoughts and prayers are with his family, friends, colleagues, students, and all those whose lives he touched.”

Witnesses who spoke to NBC affiliate WXIA of Atlanta said they saw Kariem fall from the Goliath roller coaster, and at least two people said they saw him strike parts of the ride before he hit the ground.
“He fell and hit the car three different times,” a witness told the station.
The witness said that the falling man was captured in their souvenir picture taken during the ride.
He added that Kariem’s body hit others on the ride before falling onto the roof of a haunted house attraction below.
Another witness told WXIA that Kariem was on the ride with a young boy who appeared to be his son, while a woman who appeared to be his wife and a young girl watched from the ground.
A third witness told WXIA that he and his wife saw Kariem ejected from his car and bounce off the coaster three times.
“We saw it all,” the man said. “We were having a great time and just screaming, ‘Oh my God, what is happening?’” the woman said.
A park spokesperson said in a statement that it was “deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today.”
“Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends, and loved ones,” the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson added that the park was supporting guests and employees and that details would not be released immediately “out of respect for the family’s privacy.”
Logan Conner said he was on the ride with his fiancé when he saw Kariem come out of his seat on Goliath.
“The man started levitating in the air sideways,” he said. “We made direct eye contact with him.”
Nicholas Mendenhall told the “TODAY” show he rode the roller coaster with his son 10 minutes prior to the incident.

“He came up out of his car, he was in his seat, and went forward and just came down headfirst,” he said. “It was in slow motion. And there was a moment where I was like, ‘God just let this man stay in that cart.’ It all happened so fast.”
Add to Google
Add to Google
Video showed riders exiting the roller coaster after it paused mid-ride and were forced to walk down a steep incline.

Goliath, designed and built by Bolliger & Mabillard Consulting Engineers of Switzerland, opened in 2006 and features a drop of more than 200 feet and speeds of at least 70 mph, which places it in the category of a hyper coaster.
A Six Flags spokesperson said by email Monday night that it has temporarily closed nine similar rides at the company’s other North American locations “out of an abundance of caution.”
Father describes fatal roller coaster incident

Those rides include Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America; Goliath at Six Flags Magic Mountain; Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure; Leviathan and Behemoth at Canada’s Wonderland; Fury 325 and Thunder Striker at Carowinds; and Orion and Diamondback at Kings Island, the spokesperson said.
The company did not provide any more details on when the rides will reopen.

In September, Six Flags was named in multiple lawsuits after riders alleged they suffered brain injuries on the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California. It includes 360-degree rotating seats, a 215-foot drop and sudden flips and rotations.
That coaster has been closed since July 12, a day after attorney Christopher Bulone said one of the plaintiffs suffered catastrophic brain injury after a ride.
Magic Mountain President Brian Oerding said in a Sept. 29 statement that X2 was being retired because “it’s the right thing to do” after guest confidence in its safety was affected.
Six Flags Over Georgia is about 10 miles west of downtown Atlanta.

title: Decorated San Francisco police officer and her daughter killed by her husband in suspected murder-suicide
summary: So far, investigators haven’t determined why former police Sgt. Kevin Mannix killed his wife, Ann Mannix, a former deputy chief, and their 24-year-old daughter.
story: The San Francisco Police Department was in mourning Tuesday after a trailblazing police officer and her husband, who also had  worked for the department, were found dead along with their daughter in what investigators are calling a “suspected double-murder suicide.”

Retired Sgt. Kevin Mannix, 68, fatally shot his wife, Ann Mannix, 64, a retired deputy chief, and their 24-year-old daughter, Katherine Elizabeth Mannix, around 5 p.m. Sunday before turning the gun on himself, the Marin County Sheriff’s Office said.
Police found their bodies after responding to a home in a neighborhood just north of the city following a 911 call from a person “who safely exited the residence.”
Investigators have not released a motive for the mayhem, and autopsies were scheduled Tuesday for all three people.
Meanwhile, the San Francisco PD was trying to absorb the loss.

“The tragic loss of retired Deputy Chief Ann Mannix, her daughter Katie, and retired Sergeant Kevin Mannix in a suspected murder-suicide has left our entire SFPD family reeling,” the San Francisco Police Officers Association said in a statement posted online. “There are no words that can fully capture the depth of this tragedy, nor are there simple answers to the painful questions we are all asking.”
Kevin Mannix worked for the SFPD for 27 years before retiring from the department in 2018 with the rank of sergeant, according to the department.
For Subscribers
But it was his wife who left the biggest mark on the department.
For Subscribers

A fourth-generation San Franciscan with several relatives who had previously worked as police officers, Ann Mannix joined the SFPD in 1986, a little over a decade after it started to hire women as patrol officers, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.
Ann Mannix rose steadily through the ranks, from lieutenant in 2003 to commander in 2015 and to deputy chief in 2018.

Before retiring in 2021, she led the field operations and special operations bureaus, the police department said in a statement. And she was the first woman to be part of and later lead the SWAT team.

title: Trump rally protester attacked in act of ‘senseless’ political violence, Ohio mayor says
summary: “It must be emphatically stated that senseless (political) violence has absolutely NO place in our community or in our democratic process,” Youngstown Mayor Derrick McDowell said.
story: At least two men attending President Donald Trump’s rally in Ohio attacked a female protester in a “senseless” confrontation decried by the mayor of Youngstown on Tuesday.

A pair of men, one in an adjustable baseball cap and a bald man in a dark T-shirt, put hands on a woman Monday during the GOP event inside Covelli Centre in Youngstown, multiple videos of the incident showed.
The man in a blue baseball cap pawed at the woman, wearing a shirt reading “Release the Epstein Files,” and pushed her down before the balding man jumped on her.
He appeared to throw multiple punches at the woman’s face, pull her hair and put her in a headlock before uniformed law enforcement officers arrived to take her away.

title: Federal judge issues longer-term decision blocking Trump’s White House media ban
summary: U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued an injunction preventing CNN, Politico and MS NOW from being booted from the White House grounds until the case is decided.
story: A federal judge issued an order late Tuesday blocking the Trump administration from banning CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House complex while the organizations’ lawsuit over access proceeds.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly of Washington, D.C., issued the preliminary injunction in the wake of a hearing Thursday at which the administration contended it imposed the ban in part because of national security concerns; media organizations said it was because of “viewpoint discrimination.”

Kelly sided with the news outlets, noting that Trump used national security as a reason for the ban after their press passes had already been revoked and ruling that it also likely violated reporters’ freedom of speech and due process rights.

“There is practically nothing national security-related in the record connected to the President’s decision to revoke Plaintiffs’ hard passes to which the Court can defer,” Kelly wrote in his 26-page opinion.

His order will give the outlets access to the White House until the underlying lawsuit challenging the ban is resolved. But it doesn’t require the administration to allow reporters from the outlets access to the Oval Office or Air Force One — locations where the administration has blocked reporters from CNN and Politico in recent weeks.
Trump vowed to appeal on Truth Social before the ruling was handed down. The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment following the ruling.
Kelly had issued a temporary restraining order lifting the ban while he weighed whether to issue an injunction.
Trump announced the bans of CNN, MS NOW and Politico on social media on Sept. 18, saying they were a “result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he wrote on Truth Social.
In court filings, the three news organizations said the ban affected 78 journalists who had “hard passes,” meaning they had been previously screened and credentialed to work at the White House.
The outlets filed a lawsuit alleging Trump’s action violated their due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the suit said.

The White House and Trump then began arguing that the ban was intended to address national security concerns, with Trump saying in another post that the outlets’ reporting was “a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”
For Subscribers
The judge was unmoved by that argument.
Kelly said it was clear from Trump’s announcement of the ban and from subsequent remarks that his motivation was content.

“President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him,” Kelly wrote, finding this decision violated the journalists’ First and Fifth amendment rights.

He noted, however, that his decision doesn’t concede that Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness are unfounded or that the government is “powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.”
For Subscribers

Kelly cited Trump’s recent remarks to Time magazine that he didn’t like “bad story after bad story” coming from CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists. It was, Ted Boutrous, the news outlets’ attorney, had argued ahead of the decision, “a confession of what amounts to viewpoint discrimination.”
“President Trump, I’ll give him credit,” Boutrous said. “He’s not hiding it.”
In his previous decision, Kelly also found that the administration had denied the outlets due process under settled law from several cases that have made their way to the D.C. federal appeals court.
The White House argued that the appeals court decisions were wrong.
“Maybe—but this Court is bound by D.C. Circuit precedent, full stop,” Kelly wrote.

At a hearing on the injunction Thursday, the Justice Department lawyer representing the White House, Michael Velchik, asked Kelly to lift his restraining order, calling the White House a “sacred place” that shouldn’t have to give people access just because they “identify as a reporter.”
“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” Velchik said.

Boutrous argued that the administration was engaging in impermissible and unconstitutional “viewpoint discrimination” because the ban was based on Trump’s dislike of the outlets’ reporting and because he has said he hoped the ban would force journalists to “straighten themselves out.”
In court filings, Boutrous urged Kelly to ignore the national security arguments, saying they were manufactured and not what the case is really about.

Boutrous argued that “the President himself has continued telling anyone who will listen precisely what this ban is really about, most recently complaining at length in an interview with Time magazine that he banned Plaintiffs because he feels that he should not ‘be forced to bear’ what he considers ‘constantly bad stories,’ as he ‘won the election’ and has ‘done great things.’”
After Tuesday night’s ruling, Boutrous said he and his clients were grateful to the court for securing their access anew.

“The President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like,” he said in a statement. “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban.’”

Separately, the Justice Department said last week that it was investigating five major TV networks, including CNN and NBC, for potentially violating federal antitrust laws after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of Trump as a result of the ban against the three news outlets.

The pool is a rotating group of networks that share the duties of recording a president’s activities during public appearances and travel. The on-duty network then distributes information and media, such as video and audio, to other outlets for their use.

title: Judge extends order blocking Trump administration from clearing trees at D.C. golf course
summary: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes handed down the order one day after she accused the administration of duping her in order to chop down over 400 trees.
story: The judge presiding over a court fight involving President Donald Trump’s plans to redo a public golf course in Washington, D.C., issued an order Tuesday temporarily barring the administration from knocking down more trees at the site.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes handed down the order a day after an emergency hearing in which she accused the government of engaging in deception to knock down more than 400 trees at the East Potomac Golf Links over the holiday weekend.
“The Court ORDERS that Defendants may not fell any further trees on the East Potomac Golf Course through Monday, October 26,” the judge wrote in a directive posted on the docket.

Reyes is overseeing a lawsuit filed by a preservation group and two Washington residents challenging Trump’s golf course renovation. Earlier this year, she denied the plaintiffs’ request for a restraining order in the case after administration lawyers assured her they would give her and the plaintiffs ample notice of any large-scale work being done on the course.

On Friday, attorneys for the Justice Department said in court papers filed shortly before 5 p.m. that the National Park Service would be removing roughly 500 trees from the course over the three-day holiday weekend. That work started Saturday morning, a park official testified in court Monday, and 430 trees were knocked down.

The official, National Mall and Memorial Parks Superintendent Kevin Griess, said workers had identified about 300 more trees that still need to be cut down, but they weren’t able to work Sunday because of bad weather.
Reyes told lawyers for the Justice Department at the hearing that she was “furious” with the government.
“I was hearing from everyone on plaintiffs’ side this was going to happen. I said repeatedly, ‘No, I trust the government.’ I trusted you all not to do precisely what you have done,” the judge said.
“What has happened has cost the government all of its credibility,” Reyes added.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The administration argued in a filing Friday that the work was for “maintenance activities” that were unrelated to Trump’s plans to transform the 100-year-old course into championship-style greens. It said it was implementing recommendations from a 2019 “Cultural Landscape Report” aimed at restoring the course closer to its original design.

The plaintiffs, which include the D.C. Preservation League, scoffed at the argument in court papers, saying that there would have been no mad scramble to implement a years-old plan — and noting that Trump’s plan for the site would “require massive tree-clearing.”

“Defendants would have this Court believe that this unprecedented operation is merely the sudden and purely coincidental fulfillment of recommendations posited in a Cultural Landscape Report seven years ago and is totally unrelated to the ongoing implementation of the Washington National plan,” they wrote.
“Even if Defendants were entitled to the benefit of the doubt, they are not entitled to a suspension of disbelief,” they said.

Reyes has demanded to know how the decision to chop down the trees came together. She initially ordered a follow-up hearing with testimony from a top official at the Interior Department on Tuesday but issued an order in the morning delaying the hearing until next Monday. She also directed National Park Service acting Director Jessica Bowron to appear.

Reyes, a Biden-appointed judge, had made clear at a hearing last month that she’d been hoping to avoid issuing a restraining order in the case. “I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees. I am a judge,” she said then.

title: NFL legend Terry Bradshaw says he realizes his TV career is ‘coming to an end’
summary: Bradshaw made the comments speaking with NBC News about his new memoir, “Looking for Terry.”
story: Pro Football Hall of Famer and Fox broadcaster Terry Bradshaw told NBC News on Tuesday his television career is winding down.
“I realize my time on television as a sports broadcaster is coming to an end,” Bradshaw, 78, said on “NBC News Daily” as he was discussing his new memoir, “Looking for Terry.”
Bradshaw was asked about his busy schedule when he made the remark; in addition to his writing, he has a horse ranch, a bourbon line and several grandchildren.
“I just love life. Billy Graham said, and I never forgot this quote, he said, ‘The day you retire is the day you start dying,’” Bradshaw said.
He added, “I’m a workaholic; I love to work,” before he said he knew he was nearing the end of his broadcasting career.
Bradshaw began his career as an analyst in 1984, the year he retired. He was a color commentator for CBS until he joined its pregame show in 1990.

In 1994, Bradshaw joined Fox, and he has appeared on its Sunday pregame show ever since. He and Howie Long are the only two members of the show who have been on the “Fox NFL Sunday” desk since its inception.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Bradshaw, a Louisiana native, spent all of his storied playing career with the Pittsburgh Steelers, quarterbacking the legendary franchise from 1970 through 1983. He played in only one game his final season, retiring because of elbow troubles.

Bradshaw led the Steelers to four Super Bowl wins from 1974 to 1979, becoming the first quarterback in NFL history to win three (as well as four) Super Bowls. He was named Super Bowl MVP twice and also won a regular-season MVP award in 1978.
Bradshaw was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1989, and no Pittsburgh player has worn his iconic No. 12 since he retired.

In addition to his broadcasting career, Bradshaw has spent part of his post-playing days as an actor. He appeared in television shows such as the sitcom “Everybody Loves Raymond” and the fantasy football comedy “The League,” and he even participated in “The Masked Singer.”
In 2006, Bradshaw played the father of Matthew McConaughey’s character in the romantic comedy “Failure to Launch,” appearing nude in one scene.

In his memoir, Bradshaw also discusses some of the personal issues he has faced in retirement, including battling cancer and depression.
“I couldn’t understand why I had this horrible sinking feeling, and I was so miserable,” Bradshaw said of dealing with depression.
He added that it was difficult as a former NFL player to open up about his mental health issues, saying a good friend of his even once made fun of him for discussing his depression in the past.
“It was a hard thing for me to decide to do, because I didn’t want it to be taken lightly, and I didn’t want to be laughed at,” Bradshaw said.
He added: “A lot of men think if they dealt with depression that people are going to see it as a weakness. It’s a disease. It’s a disconnect.”

title: What to Know About ‘Breaking Bad’ Actor RJ Mitte’s Cause of Death and Cerebral Palsy Diagnosis
summary: RJ Mitte, “Breaking Bad” actor, died of suicide, his representatives said about his cause of death. What the actor said about living with cerebral palsy.
story: RJ Mitte was one of the emotional centers of “Breaking Bad,” playing a teenager with cerebral palsy, a condition he lived with in real life since he was a toddler.
The actor passed away at 34.
Nonprofit United Cerebral Palsy said it was “heartbroken by the loss” of Mitte, who was an ambassador for organization, noting his death was “deeply felt across the disability community.”
“We knew him as someone who brought kindness, humor, and genuine warmth to every interaction,” said Susan Sellers, president and CEO of UCP, in a statement.

Bryan Cranston, who played his father on the hit TV show, wrote in an Instagram post that he was in “deep despair.” He recalled Mitte was 14 when he was cast as his son, a role “he played with joy and enthusiasm.”
“Born with Cerebral Palsy, he never — ever — allowed that challenge to be an excuse for anything. He met the demanding shooting schedule head on with great determination,” Cranston wrote.
Actor Bob Odenkirk, who played attorney Saul Goodman on “Breaking Bad,” called Mitte a “good person who shared his personal story and his time to help out others.”
“Whenever I saw him, he was meeting the world with positivity and a strong desire to connect,” Odenkirk told People. “This is simply, deeply sad.”
RJ Mitte’s Cause of Death
Mitte died on Monday, Oct. 12, in Brownsville, Texas, where he had moved, the local Justice of the Peace Judge Cyndi Hinojosa told NBC News.
“Sadly, we can confirm that suicide was the cause of death,” Sean Reilly, his representative, said in a statement to NBC News on Tuesday, Oct. 13.
“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” his reps previously said.
Mitte lived with cerebral palsy and drew from his own experience to bring authenticity to his “Breaking Bad” role and build “a platform on disability awareness and inclusion,” they added.
What RJ Mitte Said About His Cerebral Palsy
The actor was diagnosed with cerebral palsy at around 3 years old, and underwent physical, occupational and speech therapy, he told Vice in 2016.

“People perceive disability as a weakness, as an illness, as something that needs to be cured, and we have to fight against that,” Mitte noted. “Someone said, ‘What’s wrong with you?’ And I was like, ‘What’s wrong with me? What’s wrong with you? I’m fine, man.’”

As a child, Mitte was a severe toe walker so part of the treatment involved doctors bending his foot as far as it would go and putting it in a cast, “which was not fun,” he recalled. A few weeks later, the cast would be taken off, his foot bent even further and immobilized in a cast again — a process that was repeated until his foot was flat.
“I’m always working at taking control. It’s a fight. It will always be a fight,” he said about his body.

“Breaking Bad” showed real characters that everyone could relate to, Mitte noted. He played the son of Walter White — a high school chemistry teacher who starts making and selling crystal meth as a way to secretly make more money for his family after he’s diagnosed with terminal cancer.
Mitte’s teenage character was based on a real person with cerebral palsy who was friends with the show’s creator, Mitte said on The Joe Vulpis Podcast a week before his death.
The actor kept the forearm crutches his character used in “Breaking Bad.” That was the only thing he “truly wanted” from the set, Mitte said, though he didn’t use them in real life.
The actor was reluctant to become an advocate at first, but found himself naturally doing advocacy work. He created an anti-bullying campaign and took part in philanthropic work.
“I’m lucky that I can be an advocate, I’m lucky that I can do what I do. … I think we all have an obligation to have an impact for the positive,” he said.

Mitte understood the power of visibility, United Cerebral Palsy said, noting that “when entertainment, education, and public life represent people with disabilities authentically, it can challenge stereotypes and expand what others believe is possible.”
Asked how people with disabilities can remove the stigma of not being able-bodied, Mitte urged others to be open.

“Don’t hide your disability. Don’t hide whatever it is that you’re hiding — and I’m not just talking about a physical disability, I’m talking about a mental disability. Show who you are and what you are to the world,” he said.
In 2025, the actor got engaged to his longtime girlfriend after he proposed during a fundraising gala for United Cerebral Palsy of San Diego, People reported.
“I’m thrilled to have found my person, my partner in life who makes me want to be better, no matter what we’re doing,” he said about his engagement.
What Is Cerebral Palsy?

It’s a group of neurologic disorders caused when a baby’s brain is damaged, usually as it develops in the womb, disrupting a child’s ability to control muscles and movement, and maintain posture and balance, according to the National Library of Medicine.
While most people with cerebral palsy have the condition at birth, it may not be diagnosed until months or years later, the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke explains.
Symptoms depend on how the condition affects the body — it can cause arm or leg weakness, stiff muscles, involuntary movements and other problems.
There are many different types and levels of disability, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
“A person with severe CP might need to use special equipment to be able to walk or might not be able to walk at all and might need lifelong care,” the CDC notes.
“A person with mild CP, on the other hand, might walk a little awkwardly, but might not need any special help.”
Mitte had mild cerebral palsy and stopped wearing leg braces at 13, he told L.A. Parent. But his character in “Breaking Bad” used forearm crutches.
There’s no cure for cerebral palsy, but treatment such as physical therapy, medication, surgery and mobility devices can help people manage their symptoms.

title: Fan Favorite Couple Takes Their Last Bow During ‘DWTS’ Super Bowl Night
summary: The “Dancing With the Stars” ballroom felt the team spirit as it celebrated Super Bowl Night.
story: The “Dancing With the Stars” ballroom felt the team spirit as it celebrated Super Bowl Night.
For the Oct. 13 episode, the remaining 11 couples performed to songs that were “made famous” by some of the most iconic Super Bowl performances.

The sports-filled night began with an exhilarating opening number set to Bad Bunny’s “NUEVAYoL,” “Rude Boy” by Rihanna and “HUMBLE.” by Kendrick Lamar. The routine also included appearances from NFL legends and “Dancing with the Stars” alums Donald Driver, Emmitt Smith, DeMarcus Ware and Danny Amendola.

As Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough co-hosted, Carrie Ann Inaba, Bruno Tonioli and Derek Hough were joined by “Monday Night Football” broadcaster Joe Buck, who brought his football expertise to the ballroom.
“I know absolutely nothing about dance!” Buck exclaimed. “Nothing, but I married a dancer.”
Buck then gave wife Michelle Beisner-Buck, a reporter, sports commentator and former NFL cheerleader, who was in the audience, a shout out.

title: The Kelly Clarkson Store Debacle, Unpacked by a Crisis PR Pro
summary: A disgruntled Kelly Clarkson, a curiosity shop in Brooklyn and an animatronic bird named Molly have collided to create a drama that has divided the internet.
story: A disgruntled Kelly Clarkson, a curiosity shop in Brooklyn and an animatronic bird named Molly have collided to create a drama that has divided the internet.

Complaints posted on X by the Grammy-winning singer have been countered by the store’s version of events when it comes to whether a $15,000 mechanical bird puppet was for sale when Clarkson visited recently.
Clarkson and a store named Art of Play each posted twice in a back-and-forth about what they believe happened, leaving everyone else to decide which side was in the right.
Clarkson is a host on “The Voice” and the former host of “The Kelly Clarkson Show,” both of which aired on NBC. NBC is a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of TODAY.
TODAY.com spoke with Evan Nierman, CEO of Manhattan-based crisis PR firm Red Banyan, about how the situation could’ve been avoided and whether there is a winner or loser in all of this.
Here’s how a public relations professional looks at it.
The Store’s Response to Clarkson’s Initial Post Was Too ‘Snarky’

The conflict began when Clarkson posted on X on Oct. 10 that she was shopping at Art of Play in Brooklyn, asked about an item and was “looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me.”
She compared her experience to Julia Roberts’ character in “Pretty Woman,” who is dismissed by a condescending saleswoman while shopping at a Beverly Hills boutique because she is dressed casually.

Art of Play answered in an Instagram post on Oct. 11 in which it said the animatronic bird named Molly was not for sale, but the artist who created it had a “twin” that he would be willing to sell to Clarkson for $15,000.
Nierman said the store’s initial response was on the right track before derailing at the end.
The 1 Part of Clarkson’s Response That Didn’t Help Her at All
Following Art of Play’s Instagram post, Clarkson responded with a second post on X saying that the store’s claim that the animatronic bird named Molly was not for sale was a lie.
Clarkson wrote that she was told it was for sale for $15,000 and a salesperson implied she didn’t have the money and suggested a “comparable” item, which Art of Play disputed in its response.
The singer attached an out-of-focus photo of the bird that she claimed showed it had a price tag on it, which obviously made it for sale.

“When she attached a blurry, unreadable image of what was purported to be a price tag, I don’t think it helped her at all,” Nierman said. “It was not her picture, it was taken somewhere else. I don’t think you can point to that with any confidence that she had a smoking gun of evidence. If she had photographed it herself while she was at the store, that would have been a completely different discussion.”
What the Store Could’ve Done to Avoid the Situation
Nierman saw a simple way to avoid the whole confrontation altogether: Just sell Clarkson the animatronic bird.

“I think the store went a little overboard in trying to emphasize that Molly couldn’t be bought by anyone, which was a misstep,” he said. “If you have a customer who’s willing to pay an exorbitant amount of money, and you know there’s a twin out there, sell the person the mechanical bird, get the twin and mount that one. They missed a huge opportunity to just make a customer happy, and that’s not the person you want to piss off.”
Is There a Winner and a Loser in All This?
Both sides are sticking to their story, so there may never be a resolution.

“No side has a monopoly on the truth when they’re so entrenched in their position,” he said. “The only people who really know what happened are Kelly, the sales associate and Molly the mechanical bird, and I don’t think we’re going to get a clear answer from Molly.”
There also doesn’t appear to be a clear winner in all the drama.

“I don’t think either side comes off smelling of roses from this dispute, but at the same time neither is going to suffer irreparable harm,” Nierman said. “Clarkson is rich, famous, and beloved by legions of fans who will have her back no matter what and will come to her defense.

“The store likely has its own customer base, which is not comprised chiefly of Kelly Clarkson’s X followers, so I suspect they will be fine. It’s even possible the store will end up garnering extra support from MVP customers or people in the neighborhood who thought the store was treated unfairly.”
One thing is for sure, Nierman says: The two will forever be linked together.
